title: APIs
subtitle: Design stable service contracts, resource models, pagination, and failure responses
objectives: Explain what an API is and why a boundary beats direct database access
Design RESTful resource URLs and know why nouns beat verbs
Paginate, version, and return errors the way production systems do
Reason about chattiness, over-fetching, and when REST, GraphQL, or gRPC wins

exercises.title: An API defines how one program requests work from another
exercises.body: An Application Programming Interface (API) specifies allowed operations, required inputs, returned data, and errors. A weather app sends an HTTP request to a forecast API; the provider validates it, reads its own systems, and returns a structured response such as JSON.
exercises.note: Changing a published field's meaning or type can break deployed clients. Providers usually add compatible fields, deprecate gradually, or introduce a new version.

exercises.prompt: A mobile screen calls three backend services serially. Add a backend-for-frontend that calls them in parallel.
exercises.beforeStatus: SCREEN DATA · 3 serial mobile round trips × 80ms = at least 240ms
exercises.afterStatus: SCREEN DATA · 1 mobile round trip; backend fan-out finishes near the slowest call
exercises.result: The serial mobile round trips collapsed into one
exercises.why: A backend-for-frontend can replace several high-latency mobile round trips with one request and parallel server-side fan-out. Its latency still includes the slowest dependency and its own processing overhead.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the system for this case: A mobile screen calls three backend services serially. Add a backend-for-frontend that calls them in parallel. Place Mobile BFF, Profile, Orders. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Mobile app → Mobile BFF; Mobile BFF → Profile; Mobile BFF → Orders; Mobile BFF → Offers. That topology is the evidence for the answer: A backend-for-frontend can replace several high-latency mobile round trips with one request and parallel server-side fan-out. Its latency still includes the slowest dependency and its own processing overhead.

exercises.prompt: Your weather app shows tomorrow's forecast. It doesn't own any weather satellites. How does it get the data?
choices: It calls someone else's API and asks for it
The data ships inside the app
It reads the weather company's database directly
exercises.why: An Application Programming Interface (API) gives the weather app a defined request it can send to a weather service and a defined response it can consume. The provider can collect and manage forecast data while exposing only the supported operations.

exercises.prompt: An API is essentially a ______ between two programs: ask me this way, and I'll answer that way.
exercises.why: An API contract specifies valid operations, inputs, authentication, response shapes, and errors. Clients code against those guarantees, so incompatible contract changes can break deployed integrations.

exercises.prompt: Why doesn't the weather company just let your app read their database directly?
choices: Direct database access would be faster and better
An API hides their internals, enforces rules, and lets them change their database without breaking you
Databases physically can't be read by other programs
There's no real reason — it's just tradition
exercises.why: The API exposes controlled operations while hiding the provider’s schema and storage implementation. This boundary lets the provider validate input, authorize callers, enforce limits, and change internal databases without granting clients direct storage access.

exercises.prompt: Match each piece of an API to its job.

pairs.right: A specific address you can call
Identifies or authenticates the client presenting it

exercises.why: The endpoint identifies an operation address, JSON defines the exchanged data representation, an API key identifies or authenticates the client presenting that bearer credential, and documentation records the contract. A copied key proves possession, not a human identity, and authorization still decides what that client may do.

exercises.prompt: Order what happens in one API call.
steps: Server checks the API key and validates the request
Server fetches the data it needs
exercises.why: The server authenticates and validates the request before doing expensive or privileged work. It then obtains the forecast and serializes it as JSON, which the app parses before rendering the result.

exercises.prompt: Why did JSON become the default format for web APIs, beating XML?
choices: It's human-readable and maps directly onto data structures most languages already have
It's much older and more established
exercises.why: JSON maps directly to common language structures such as objects, arrays, strings, and numbers, and its text form is easy to inspect. Binary formats can reduce payload size and parsing cost when internal services prioritize efficiency over human readability.

exercises.title: Resource-oriented HTTP APIs separate identity from operation
exercises.body: A resource path identifies data: `/users/42` names one user and `/users/42/orders` names that user's order collection. The HTTP method supplies standard operation semantics: `GET` retrieves, `POST` submits, `PUT` replaces, and `DELETE` removes.
exercises.note: Standard method semantics let clients, gateways, and caches handle requests correctly. For example, `GET` is defined as safe and idempotent.

exercises.prompt: A mobile home screen makes six sequential API calls at 80ms each. Add a screen-specific endpoint that fetches the same independent data in parallel.
choices: Add a BFF that calls dependencies in parallel
Cache every user's home screen for one hour
choiceFeedback: A larger timeout tolerates the 480ms chain but does not remove its sequential waits.
The BFF collapses client round trips and overlaps independent dependency waits.
A long shared cache policy risks serving personalized data to the wrong user and does not fit frequently changing screens.
exercises.afterStatus: DATA WAIT · 6 parallel calls · about 80ms plus overhead
exercises.result: The client crossed the network once and backend fan-out ran concurrently
exercises.why: A backend-for-frontend can aggregate data for one client screen and issue independent downstream requests concurrently. The slowest dependency now sets the fan-out latency, so timeouts and partial-failure behavior must be explicit.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: A mobile home screen makes six sequential API calls at 80ms each. Add a screen-specific endpoint that fetches the same independent data in parallel. Place Home BFF, 6 APIs. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Mobile app → Home BFF; Home BFF → 6 APIs. That topology is the evidence for the answer: A backend-for-frontend can aggregate data for one client screen and issue independent downstream requests concurrently. The slowest dependency now sets the fan-out latency, so timeouts and partial-failure behavior must be explicit.

exercises.prompt: Which URL is the better-designed way to fetch user 42?
exercises.why: `/users/42` names user 42 as a resource, while the `GET` method already expresses retrieval. Keeping actions in HTTP methods produces a consistent resource model across create, read, replace, and delete operations.

exercises.prompt: Match each request to what it should do.
exercises.why: The collection path `/users` supports listing with `GET` and creation with `POST`. The member path `/users/42` identifies one user for retrieval or deletion, so the method changes while the resource address stays stable.

exercises.prompt: You want to list the orders belonging to user 42. Which is the RESTful design?
exercises.why: `/users/42/orders` represents the orders subordinate to user 42, so the path encodes the ownership relation and the method can encode the operation. Deeply nested paths should be limited when resources also need independent identities.

exercises.prompt: Which of these are good REST practices? Select all.
choices: Put the action verb in the URL (`/createUser`)
Use HTTP methods to express the action
exercises.why: Plural resource names, HTTP methods for actions, and accurate status codes form a predictable interface. An action such as creation belongs in `POST` semantics, so `/createUser` duplicates intent in the path.

exercises.prompt: REST APIs are stateless. What does that demand of every single request?
choices: Each request carries the context needed to interpret it; the server does not rely on conversational context from earlier requests
exercises.why: REST statelessness forbids server-held conversational client context that the next request needs for interpretation. The service may still persist users, orders, and shared session records as resource state; the next request supplies its credentials, target, and inputs so any compatible server can handle it.

exercises.prompt: In REST, URLs name ______, and HTTP methods express the action.
exercises.why: A REST URL identifies a resource such as `/users/42`, and the HTTP method states the requested operation on it. This separation lets one stable address support several standard operations.

exercises.title: Pagination bounds the work and payload of a collection request
exercises.body: Pagination bounds response work. Offset pages can shift under inserts. A cursor should encode a stable total order, such as `(created_at, id)`: the unique `id` breaks timestamp ties, so the next query can continue strictly after one exact row.
exercises.note: A cursor stabilizes page boundaries, not the whole dataset. Without snapshot semantics, later updates or deletes can still change what appears across the traversal. Enforce a server-side page maximum.

exercises.prompt: `GET /users` tries to return all 50 million users in one response. What breaks?
choices: Nothing — it's just a big response
Almost everything: a huge payload, a brutal database query, timeouts, and memory blowups on both ends
exercises.why: Returning all 50 million rows creates unbounded database work, response memory, transfer time, and client parsing cost. As the collection grows, one request can exhaust limits or time out, so the endpoint needs a bounded result size.

exercises.prompt: Each user row is about 2KB, the endpoint has a 1MB response budget, and latency degrades above 200 rows. What continuation contract should the server enforce?
choices: Honor any client `limit` because callers know their needs
Cap pages at 200 rows and return an opaque cursor for the next page
Return 500 rows because their raw size is exactly 1MB
Use compression and remove the page limit
exercises.why: A 200-row cap stays below both the measured latency limit and the 1MB raw-payload ceiling, leaving room for envelope and encoding overhead. An opaque cursor continues the traversal without exposing storage details, and the server-side cap prevents a caller from creating unbounded query and serialization work.

exercises.prompt: Your feed paginates with `?offset=1000000&limit=20`. Two real problems appear at scale. Which describes them?
choices: Offset pagination is always faster but uses more memory
Deep offsets get slow (the database must walk past every skipped row), and new inserts shift rows so users see duplicates or miss items
There are no problems — offset is the standard
exercises.why: A deep `OFFSET` may scan and discard many preceding rows, while inserts can shift positions between requests. A cursor over an indexed total order such as `(created_at, id)` continues after one exact row; a timestamp alone is unsafe when several rows share it. Without a snapshot, later changes can still affect later pages.

exercises.prompt: You need to change what a field means in your public API. Third-party apps depend on it. What do you do?
choices: Version the API (`/v2`) or add a new field, while keeping the old behavior working
Delete the endpoint and start over
Change it, but email everyone first
exercises.why: Changing an existing field’s meaning violates the contract already implemented by third-party clients. A new field or version preserves old behavior while clients migrate, allowing incompatible semantics to coexist during the transition.

exercises.prompt: Which of these changes would BREAK existing clients? Select all.
choices: Adding a new optional field to the response
Changing a field's type from string to number
exercises.why: Removing, renaming, or changing the type of a field invalidates code that expects the old response schema. A new optional field is generally compatible because tolerant clients can ignore an unknown member.

exercises.prompt: Your API returns `200 OK`, with `{"error": "user not found"}` in the body. Why is that a bad idea?
choices: It isn't — the error is right there in the body
It lies: caches, monitoring, retries, and client error handling all key off the status code, so a `200` hides the failure
exercises.why: `200 OK` tells clients, caches, and monitoring that the request succeeded, so embedding an error only in the body produces contradictory machine signals. `404 Not Found` plus a consistent error object makes both transport status and application detail accurate.

exercises.title: The N+1 problem turns one list read into one request per item
exercises.body: An N+1 request pattern fetches a list with one call, then issues N related calls to render its N items. For a post list, the client may fetch posts once and request each author separately. The total is `1 + N` network requests for one screen.
exercises.note: If the related calls run sequentially, latency grows with N. If they run concurrently, connection usage and downstream load rise with N instead.

exercises.prompt: Show the minimum components and flows that implement this mechanism: The N+1 problem turns one list read into one request per item
exercises.why: An N+1 request pattern fetches a list with one call, then issues N related calls to render its N items. For a post list, the client may fetch posts once and request each author separately. The total is `1 + N` network requests for one screen. If the related calls run sequentially, latency grows with N. If they run concurrently, connection usage and downstream load rise with N instead.

exercises.prompt: A mobile screen shows 20 posts, each with its author's name. The app calls `GET /posts`, then `GET /users/{id}` for each post. How many requests is that?
exercises.why: The client performs one request for posts and 20 requests for their authors, producing 21 requests. This N+1 pattern multiplies network and server overhead; returning posts with the required author fields can collapse the screen load into one client round trip.

exercises.prompt: Your `/users` endpoint returns a 40-field object, but the mobile list screen only needs name and avatar. What's the problem called?
choices: Over-fetching — you're burning bandwidth and battery shipping fields nobody uses
exercises.why: Over-fetching sends 40 fields when the screen consumes only two, increasing transfer, parsing, and memory costs. A field-selectable API or a tailored endpoint can return the representation required by that client.

exercises.prompt: A company controls web, iOS, and Android clients. Each screen needs a different nested slice of the same graph, and the team wants one typed schema. Which requirements genuinely favor GraphQL? Select all.
choices: Clients need to select different field sets and nested relationships
One typed schema should drive validation and client tooling
Every response must use ordinary shared HTTP cache keys with no extra cache machinery
Untrusted callers must be allowed unlimited query depth and cost
exercises.why: GraphQL lets controlled clients select fields and traverse relationships through one typed schema, which fits diverse first-party screens. Because many queries share an endpoint, shared HTTP caching needs an explicit keying strategy. Production servers also bound depth, complexity, and resolver fan-out to control execution cost.

exercises.prompt: A public product API exposes stable resources to unknown third parties. It needs ordinary HTTP caching, simple per-endpoint cost limits, and no caller-defined nested queries. Which interface best fits those stated constraints?
choices: Browser clients calling internal gRPC services directly
exercises.why: Resource-oriented REST fits these requirements because methods, paths, and response metadata integrate with standard HTTP caching and endpoint-level controls. GraphQL can also be public, but its flexibility is unnecessary here and would require query-cost controls and a deliberate caching strategy.

exercises.prompt: Your public API has to survive third-party developers. Which of these protect you? Select all.
choices: Letting clients request unlimited nested data
exercises.why: Rate limits bound work per client, pagination bounds work per collection request, and versioning preserves existing contracts during evolution. Unlimited nested queries leave computation and response size controlled by callers, creating an unbounded-cost path.

exercises.prompt: Your mobile app makes 21 chatty calls per screen. Add the piece that lets it make ONE call and get a tailored response.
exercises.why: A Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) aggregates the posts and users service calls inside the datacenter and returns one mobile-specific response. The phone pays one wide-area round trip while the BFF owns internal fan-out and response shaping.

exercises.prompt: Build the mobile request path that replaces 21 wide-area calls with one. The middle component fans out inside the datacenter and shapes one mobile response.
exercises.why: The phone makes one wide-area call to a Backend-for-Frontend (BFF), which fetches posts and user data over internal links and returns only the fields the screen needs. This preserves the existing public contract; if the BFF fails or waits serially on slow dependencies, it becomes the screen's shared failure and latency point.

exercises.prompt: A music API pages through a playlist while new songs are inserted near the beginning. Which pagination contract best avoids shifting offsets and duplicated rows?
choices: Return the entire playlist every time
An opaque cursor tied to a stable ordering key
exercises.why: A cursor based on the last stable ordering key continues after a known item. Offset pages can shift when earlier rows are inserted, causing duplicates or omissions across requests.
